transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Zephyr - Head of Platform), Tom Reynolds (Zephyr SRE), Maya Chen (Zephyr CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/deck/optimize (deck), Google Sheet - cost_model_v2 (link), security package (link)

Summary (auto): Redwood Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations tailored to Zephyr Payments' latency and cost targets. Discussed hit rates, TTLs, batching windows, tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC/network considerations, and next steps for pilot benchmarking.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm sofia from redwood, i'll kick us off. daniel is our se today, he'll run through optimize recommendations around batching and the kv/prefix cache.
[00:18] Daniel: cool thanks sofia, hi aisha, tom, maya. quick agenda: why batching & kv cache matter for token cost and tail latency, how our cost model looks, demo of console settings, recommended configs for payments workloads, and pilot plan.
[00:32] Aisha: sounds good, quick context — we are running a mix right now, some requests to openai, some internal LLMs on prem. main goals: sub-200ms 95th for short prompts, keep per-inference cost predictable, and meet PCI-ish controls around logs/retention.
[00:50] Tom: yes and we need VPC connectivity, SAML SSO, and KMS integration.
[00:58] Daniel: yep all doable. to start — batching reduces per-token compute by grouping concurrent requests, continuous batching vs micro-batches — we often recommend small batching windows for low latency workloads, like 8-12ms or adaptive windows based on qps. for payments, prefix caching (aka kv cache or prefetch) gives the biggest wins if you have repeated prefixes — e.g., standard instruction prompts, headers, or user context.
[01:22] Maya: can you clarify prefix vs kv? sometimes our folks call kv cache the convo cache.
[01:27] Daniel: totally — we use prefix cache to mean storing KV cache of transformer attention states keyed by prompt prefix. kv cache is same idea; semantics vary. prefix cache is great when you have identical or highly similar prefixes across requests, reduces token compute for that prefix.
[01:41] Tom: what kind of hit rates do you need to see meaningful cost savings?
[01:45] Daniel: depends on model/seq length; rule of thumb: >20-25% hit rate starts to show clear cost delta, 40%+ is excellent. our cost model spreadsheet (shared) models hit-rate vs cost delta, and also shows how batching contributes.
[02:04] Sofia: i'll paste the sheet in chat after, but daniel, can you walk through a quick example for their workload? assume avg prompt 120 tokens with 40 token user variable tail.
[02:12] Daniel: sure. baseline: no cache, no batching, load on mpt-like or llama-ish model at x tokens/s -> cost per request is high. with a 30% prefix hit rate and a batching window tuned to 10ms for 200 qps, effective tokens computed drops ~25% in their modeled run, netting ~20-30% cost reduction. also critical is the latency interplay: larger batching windows raise median/tail latency, so we prioritize small windows for payments.
[02:44] Aisha: okay that 20-30% sounds attractive. what about dedupe & cache eviction? we can't hold cache forever.
[02:52] Daniel: yes eviction & TTLs are key. we recommend a tiered TTL strategy: short TTL (30s-2m) for ephemeral session tokens, medium (10-60m) for repeated merchant prompts, and long (hours) for static templates. also support for LRU or frequency-based eviction; Redwood console shows cache hit histograms so you can tune.
[03:14] Tom: any risks around PII or PCI? if we cache prompts with sensitive data how do we control that?
[03:20] Daniel: good call — we surface redaction hooks and policy filters. also on Dedicated or Private you can enforce no persistence of sensitive fields, integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest, and configure retention windows. we'll share SOC2/ISO docs.
[03:38] Maya: how does this change if we go Dedicated vs Hosted? we have capacity spikes end of day settlements.
[03:45] Sofia: Dedicated gives you reserved pools and predictable throughput which helps with tail latency during spikes. Hosted is simpler and cheaper at low volume but you trade control. for cost modeling we include both scenarios in the sheet — Dedicated has higher fixed cost but lower variable per-token at scale, and allows private network options.
[04:02] Daniel: also for huge spikes we recommend autoscaling policies + burst capacity. and routing policies — you can route non-critical lower-priority jobs to cheaper model variants.
[04:12] Tom: what's model quantization play here? will q4 or 4bit affect quality?
[04:16] Daniel: we typically recommend 8-bit or q4 for high-throughput scoring tasks; for generation with strict quality needs we validate via eval sets. quantization can reduce footprint by 2-4x with modest quality tradeoffs — our Optimize recommends model-specific profiles.
[04:33] Aisha: demo time?
[04:35] Daniel: yep quick tour — opening Redwood Console -> Optimize -> Batching & Caching. (screen share noises)
[04:50] Daniel: here are the key toggles: batching window (ms), max batch size, priority routing, prefix cache TTLs, and cache warming controls. you can simulate traffic in the console and it will show predicted hit rates and cost delta.
[05:08] Sofia: and that cost delta is taken from the cost model sheet we shared, which uses your historical distribution if you provide sample traffic.
[05:16] Tom: if we can't share raw traffic, can we share aggregated histograms?
[05:20] Daniel: yes aggregated sequence-length histograms + prefix fingerprint histograms are enough to model. we don't need sensitive PII.
[05:29] Maya: show us what cache warming looks like.
[05:31] Daniel: cache warming allows pre-populating KV entries for high-value prefixes ahead of anticipated spikes. e.g., during a settlement window you can precompute prefixes for the common templates and push to nodes. warming reduces first-request misses.
[05:44] Aisha: how much memory does the prefix cache cost on nodes? our infra is memory-constrained.
[05:49] Daniel: depends on model and sequence. we estimate about 100-400MB per popular prefix for larger models; the sheet has a memory vs hit-rate calc. you balance node count vs cache size.
[06:05] Tom: are cache keys global or per-shard?
[06:09] Daniel: keys are sharded with consistent hashing; within a zone requests route to the node holding the cache entry. there's a fallback to recompute if miss or eviction.
[06:18] Aisha: what's the typical lambda / throughput for maintaining small batching windows? we're worried about CPU overhead for many tiny batches.
[06:26] Daniel: the runtime uses continuous batching where grpc/socket layer aggregates requests; overhead is modest. small windows like 8-12ms at 200 qps are fine. we can also use dynamic batching which increases window when qps rises.
[06:42] Tom: can we run canaries? we want to roll this slowly.
[06:45] Sofia: absolutely — the platform supports canary rollouts by route or model version, and automatic fallback if latency SLOs degrade.
[06:56] Maya: security again — how is KMS integrated?
[07:00] Daniel: on Private/Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM) for key wrapping of cache blobs and logs. audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; retention policies configurable.
[07:16] Tom: perfect. what's a minimal pilot you'd recommend?
[07:20] Daniel: 2-week pilot, run in dedicated test pool or hosted dedicated burst, using a representative 10k qps-equivalent sample set (or scaled down sample with synthetic traffic that preserves distribution). we'll run: baseline run (no cache/batching), configured run (our recommended TTLs and 10ms batching), and a stress run for spikes. measure cost, p95 latency, error rates, and hit-rate.
[07:46] Aisha: okay and acceptance criteria?
[07:48] Sofia: say: p95 < 200ms, cost reduction >= 15% vs baseline, stable error rate under 0.1%, hit-rate above 25% for prefixes. those are negotiable but a good start.
[08:03] Daniel: i'll annotate the cost model sheet with scenarios for Zephyr — included live examples for 30% and 50% hit rates.
[08:12] Tom: question — in the sheet you model token pricing per model; what about multi-model fallbacks? sometimes we fallback to smaller models for cost.
[08:18] Daniel: we support policy-based routing: critical routes to high-quality models, non-critical to smaller/quantized variants. the cost model includes weighted mix.
[08:28] Maya: from org standpoint, who needs to be involved on our side?
[08:31] Aisha: infra (tom), platform (me), security (mike, not here), and the app teams.
[08:39] Sofia: noted. we'll include security package and an NDA addendum if needed.
[08:45] Daniel: quick caveat on transcription — sometimes tokens used for real-time streaming differ, so streaming vs non-streaming paths matter, but the cost model handles both.
[08:58] Aisha: any gotchas around eviction impacting tail latency mid-spike? like if many prefixes evict and then thrash?
[09:04] Daniel: yes that can cause a spike in compute; mitigation: set eviction thresholds conservatively, use TTL tiers, and enable cache warming before the spike. you can also reserve a small warm pool for critical prefixes.
[09:20] Tom: operationally, how do we monitor cache effectiveness?
[09:24] Daniel: console has cache hit/miss dashboards, per-prefix histograms, and token-level cost breakdowns. you can set alerts on drop in hit-rate or rising p95.
[09:34] Maya: are there legal concerns with caching user prompts? some of ours include payment references.
[09:39] Sofia: that's a policy decision; we can set rules to strip or hash sensitive fields before caching. that will reduce hit-rate somewhat but keeps compliance.
[09:50] Aisha: okay good. next steps recap?
[09:53] Sofia: i'll send pricing + the annotated cost model (Sofia). daniel will draft the pilot/benchmark plan. zephyr to send sample aggregated histograms and constraints. schedule deep dive Sept 7.
[10:06] Daniel: i'll add the recommended TTL profile: short 30-120s, medium 10-60m, long 1-6h, and model the memory tradeoffs.
[10:15] Tom: can you also include a sample ngrok/VPC diag for connectivity?
[10:19] Sofia: yes will include network diagram and SSO/KMS checklist.
[10:24] Maya: thanks team — excited to see the numbers.
[10:28] Sofia: thanks all. we'll follow up via email and update the crm. bye.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker turn counts compressed; some product names transcribed imperfectly (mpt/llama-like typed as lam-a), but content faithful.
